analysis.one_liner: Caps payday loan fees, requires free installment repayment plans, and bans criminal prosecution of borrowers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the rules for payday loans nationwide. It would have capped what lenders charge at 20 cents per dollar borrowed plus a 5% administrative fee, required lenders to let borrowers who cannot pay on time spread repayment over at least four installments with no extra fees, and banned threatening borrowers with criminal prosecution, taking their property as security, or rolling loans over more than four times. It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee and never came out; no committee vote, no floor vote, and the Congress ended without action.
analysis.who_benefits: Payday borrowers — typically low- and moderate-income workers facing a cash shortfall between paychecks. The bill would cap total loan charges at 25 cents per dollar borrowed (20 cents in interest and fees, a 5% administrative fee, and a $10 document fee), guarantee anyone who cannot pay on the due date a free extended repayment plan of at least four installments, ban threats of criminal prosecution, bar lenders from taking property as security, let borrowers cancel a loan within one business day at no cost, and limit class-action recovery — but for borrowers it would also guarantee a right to sue with penalties up to $5,000 per violation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Payday borrowers living paycheck to paycheck

how_it_helps.text: Caps what a lender can charge on a payday loan: interest and fees of no more than 20 cents per dollar borrowed, plus a 5% administrative fee and a $10 document fee, with a 20-cent-per-dollar charge allowed again on each refinance.

Requires every lender to offer, at least once every 12 months, a free extended repayment plan letting a borrower who cannot pay on the due date repay in at least four equal installments with no added interest or fees.
Prohibits lenders from threatening or seeking criminal prosecution of a borrower to collect a loan, and from taking any interest in the borrower's personal property as security.
Lets a borrower cancel a payday loan without cost by notifying the lender in writing and returning the principal by the end of the next business day.

Bans loans shorter than 7 days, more than one outstanding loan at a time, more than 4 consecutive refinancings, confession-of-judgment clauses, oppressive mandatory arbitration clauses, and the sale of any insurance with the loan; requires signed receipts after each payment.

Requires prominent written and posted warnings, including that the loan is not for long-term needs and that free credit counseling is available from NFCC-approved agencies, and gives borrowers a defense and civil penalties (up to $5,000 per violation) against violators.

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders, whose fee revenue and refinancing income would be capped, and who could no longer threaten borrowers with criminal prosecution, secure loans with personal property, or roll loans over more than four times. Borrowers in states with strict caps could also lose access to some ultra-short loans (under 7 days would be banned), though the bill expressly preserved states' ability to regulate further.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday lenders' fee and rollover revenue

drawbacks.text: The fee ceiling is high in annualized terms: lenders may charge interest and fees of 20 cents per dollar borrowed, plus a 5% administrative fee and a $10 document fee, per loan — roughly $25 per $100 on a typical short-term loan, which on a two-week loan works out to an annualized cost of several hundred percent.

The bill lets lenders refinance a payday loan up to 4 consecutive times, each time charging another 20 cents per dollar in interest and fees, so a borrower could roll over the same debt repeatedly at ongoing cost.

The bill caps total recovery in any class action or series of class actions arising from the same violation at the lesser of $500,000 or 1% of the lender's net worth, limiting the main practical tool borrowers have for challenging industry-wide practices.

The bill defines covered payday loans as closed-end loans of $2,000 or less with terms of 7 to 91 days, and expressly excludes open-end credit-card-style products, so lenders could potentially restructure products to fall outside the rules.

States may keep regulating, but their rules cannot 'significantly interfere' with a lender's ability to offer loans meeting the federal standards — a clause that could be read to limit stricter state caps that ban the high-cost loans the bill permits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers, the protections are real: an escape hatch from rollover cycles, an end to criminal-threat collection, a one-business-day rescission right, and a fee ceiling where none existed federally. But the design has serious weaknesses a supporter should acknowledge: the ceiling is set high enough that a two-week loan can still cost about $25 per $100 borrowed — roughly 650% annualized — which would legitimize nationally costs that several states ban outright, and the preemption clause could shield that pricing from stricter state rules. The class-action cap and the definition that exempts open-end and longer/larger products weaken enforcement further. Net effect: a genuine floor of protection for borrowers in states with none, purchased at the price of entrenching a high-cost lending industry nationwide.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, so it quietly died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Heath Shuler introduced the bill on May 21, 2009, joined by Representatives Minnick, Heller, and McHenry — two Democrats and two Republicans.
On the day of introduction, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never held a hearing or markup, and the bill was never reported to the House floor.
The bill attracted 35 cosponsors — 15 of the 253 House Democrats and 20 of the 178 House Republicans.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill died with it; it was never reintroduced in that session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday lenders were better off: no national fee cap, repayment-plan mandate, or collection restrictions ever took effect, so lending continued under the existing patchwork of state rules. Borrowers in states with weak laws remained exposed to rollover cycles and high fees.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Payday lenders, unaffected by any new federal rules

against.what_they_did: The payday lending industry has consistently opposed federal caps on payday loan fees and restrictions on rollovers and collection practices.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat with three Republican original cosponsors, and its 35 cosponsors split 15 Democrats and 20 Republicans; no party bloc took a recorded position because no vote was ever held.

industries.note: The bill imposes real rules — fee ceilings, mandatory installment repayment plans, bans on criminal-threat collection and repeated refinancing — that would cut into rollover-driven revenue. But it also gives the industry what it had never had: a federal statutory framework legalizing payday loans at up to roughly 25 cents per dollar per loan period nationwide, which could serve as a floor limiting stricter state rules.

The bill bans criminal prosecution threats, bars suing borrowers who enter repayment plans, and caps collectible attorney and court fees at 20% of the loan balance, cutting into aggressive collection practices aimed at low-income borrowers.
Every payday loan agreement and storefront would have to direct borrowers to NFCC-approved or government-approved credit counseling, channeling referrals to these agencies.
